title: Beyond the Person, nothing
theme: Beyond the great self is the unmanifest, beyond the unmanifest the Person; beyond the Person there is nothing — that is the limit, that the highest goal.

words.role: standard of comparison; takes up ātmā mahān of 1.3.10

words.context: Śaṅkara: the seed of the whole world, name and form not yet distinguished, «सर्वस्य जगतो बीजभूतमव्याकृतनामरूपं»; Raṅgarāmānuja (quoting the Bhāṣyakāra): the body, the chariot of 1.3.3
Śaṅkara: «पुरुषः सर्वपूरणात्», the Person because he fills all; Raṅgarāmānuja: the inner controller, the supreme Person
Śaṅkara: «निष्ठा पर्यवसानम्», the end, the culmination

sandhi.type: m before a vowel; t before p
sandhi.rule: A final m before a vowel is kept and joined to it; the final t stays before p.
A final t becomes n before the nasal n, P. 8.4.45 (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा).
The final t stays before s.

morphology.note: a-vyakta, ‘not manifest’: the negative a- with the past participle of vi-√añj, ‘to make manifest’. The Brahmasūtra (1.4.1) discusses whether the word here means the Sāṅkhya pradhāna; Śaṅkara says it does not.
Originally the post or mark at the end of a racecourse; hence ‘limit, culmination’. Feminine, so the pronoun is sā.

translation.literal: Higher than the great [self is] the unmanifest; higher than the unmanifest the Person. Higher than the Person [is] not anything; that [is] the limit, that the highest goal.
translation.readable: Beyond the great self is the unmanifest, and beyond the unmanifest the Person. Beyond the Person there is nothing at all: that is the end, that is the highest goal.

anvaya: महतः अव्यक्तम् परम् [अस्ति], अव्यक्तात् पुरुषः परः; पुरुषात् परम् किञ्चित् न [अस्ति]; सा काष्ठा, सा परा गतिः ।
syntax: Two more steps of the pattern of 1.3.10 (ablative + para- + nominative), then a negated step that closes the series, and two short nominal sentences with sā, agreeing with kāṣṭhā and gatiḥ, which name the Person as the end.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the undifferentiated seed of the world, resting in the supreme Self as the power of the banyan in its seed — «परमात्मन्योतप्रोतभावेन समाश्रितं वटकणिकायामिव वटवृक्षशक्तिः». Raṅgarāmānuja, with the Bhāṣyakāra he quotes, takes it as the body, the chariot of 1.3.3, the only element of that image the ladder has not yet named: «न रथरूपितं शरीरमिति परिशेषात् तत् अव्यक्तशब्देन उच्यते». Madhva: the goddess Ramā («ततोऽव्यक्ताभिधा रमा»).
gati can mean ‘going’ as well as ‘goal’. Śaṅkara takes up the difficulty at the start of his next comment (on 1.3.12): a goal one goes to is one from which one could return.

beginner: The ladder from the previous verse reaches its top. Beyond the great self is something called the unmanifest, and beyond that is the Person. Then the verse stops counting: there is nothing beyond the Person. That is the end of the line and the highest goal. The commentators fill in the steps differently. For Śaṅkara the unmanifest is the hidden seed from which the whole world unfolds, and the Person is the one reality that fills everything; to reach it is to know it as one's own deepest self. For Raṅgarāmānuja the unmanifest is simply the body, the chariot in the earlier picture, and the Person is the Lord who guides everything from within. For Madhva the unmanifest is the goddess Ramā and the Person is Viṣṇu. All agree that the series ends in the Person.
analogy: Like counting the rungs of a ladder up to the roof: at the roof the counting stops, because there is no further rung.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It adds two steps to the ladder — the unmanifest above the great self, the Person above the unmanifest — and then closes it: nothing is higher than the Person, who is the limit and the highest goal.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: the seed and the Person
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The unmanifest is the seed of the whole world, in which name and form are not yet distinguished: «सर्वस्य जगतो बीजभूतमव्याकृतनामरूपं». The Person is subtler and greater still, the cause of all causes, and is called puruṣa because he fills everything: «पुरुषः सर्वपूरणात्». Nothing is beyond him because he is pure consciousness and nothing else exists beside him: «यस्मान्नास्ति पुरुषाच्चिन्मात्रघनात्परं किञ्चिदपि वस्त्वन्तरम्». He is the highest goal of all who go, citing the Gītā: «‘यद्गत्वा न निवर्तन्ते’».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the body and the inner controller
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Quoting the Bhāṣyakāra, he finds every element of the chariot image named again in the ladder, so that the unmanifest must be the body: «न रथरूपितं शरीरमिति परिशेषात् तत् अव्यक्तशब्देन उच्यते इति भाषितम्». Higher than the body is the inner controller of all, the supreme Person who is the far end of the road: «सर्वान्तरात्मभूतः अन्तर्यामी अध्वनः पारभूतः परमपुरुषः». He is both the last means of control and the highest goal, «वशीकार्योपासननिवृत्त्युपायकाष्ठाभूतः परमप्राप्यश्च स एव», and controlling him means taking refuge in him: «तस्य च वशीकरणं तच्छरणागतिरेव».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: In his comment the unmanifest is Ramā and the Person Viṣṇu, whom no one equals because he is complete: «ततोऽव्यक्ताभिधा रमा । तस्यास्तु पुरुषो विष्णुः पूर्णत्वान्नैव तत्समः».

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: a goal reached by knowing
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Opening his comment on the next verse, Śaṅkara asks how there can be a goal (gati) from which there is no return, as 1.3.8 promised. He answers that the Person is everyone's inmost self, so ‘going’ to him is only a figure for knowing him: «सर्वस्य प्रत्यगात्मत्वादवगतिरेव गतिरित्युपचर्यते».

commentary.q: The verse and the Sāṅkhya debate
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Because the series mahat — avyakta — puruṣa matches Sāṅkhya terms, the Brahmasūtra (1.4.1) asks whether the verse teaches the Sāṅkhya pradhāna. Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya answers that it does not; the unmanifest is understood from the chariot image of 1.3.3. Raṅgarāmānuja reports the Bhāṣyakāra's answer to the same question in his comment on this verse.

advaita.text: The unmanifest is the undifferentiated seed of the world, resting in the supreme Self; the Person, pure consciousness, is the end of the series — «सा काष्ठा निष्ठा पर्यवसानम्» — and nothing exists beside him.

visistadvaita.text: The unmanifest is the body; the Person is the inner controller, the end of the road and the one to be reached, and refuge in him is the last of the means: «तस्य च वशीकरणं तच्छरणागतिरेव».

dvaita.text: The unmanifest is Ramā; the Person is Viṣṇu, whom nothing equals: «पूर्णत्वान्नैव तत्समः».

schools.disagreement: What the unmanifest is — the seed of the world (Śaṅkara), the body (Raṅgarāmānuja), Ramā (Madhva) — and whether the Person at the top is the one reality known as one's own Self (Śaṅkara) or the Lord distinct from the self who controls it from within (Raṅgarāmānuja, Madhva).

parallels.note: Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya takes the unmanifest here as the body of the chariot image, not the Sāṅkhya pradhāna — the reading Raṅgarāmānuja reports from his own school's Bhāṣyakāra. In his Kaṭha bhāṣya Śaṅkara explains it as the seed of the world.

parallels.quote: यद्गत्वा न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम
parallels.note: Quoted by Śaṅkara on this verse: the goal from which those who reach it do not return.

contemporary.text: Many lists of priorities never end: there is always one more thing above the last. The verse closes its list on purpose — there is nothing beyond this. Whether or not one accepts its answer, asking what one's own list would end in, and whether it ends at all, is a useful question. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: What would you put at the top of your own ladder — the thing beyond which there is nothing more important?
reflect.deeper: Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja read the same ‘unmanifest’ as the seed of the world and as the body. What does each reading make of the ladder as a whole?
reflect.practice: Write down three things you want, then ask of each: for the sake of what? Follow the answers until they stop.

references.text: Raṅgarāmānuja's comment on 1.3.10–11 quotes the Bhāṣyakāra on the ānumānika-adhikaraṇa (Brahmasūtra 1.4.1), the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa and the Gītā (18.14, 15.15, 18.61–62); these are reported as cited by him.

flags.note: Madhva's text reads paraḥ, masculine, for param, neuter, in ‘nothing is higher than the Person’ (corrections.json).
avyakta: the seed of the world (Śaṅkara, Kaṭha bhāṣya), the body of the chariot image (Raṅgarāmānuja quoting the Bhāṣyakāra; also Śaṅkara on BS 1.4.1), Ramā (Madhva).
